blocks.text: Mars is the planet next door. On a clear night you can see it. It looks like a small orange star. Mars is red because its dust is full of rust. People have sent robots to Mars. The robots drive slowly over the rocks. They dig, they take photos, and they send everything home to us.

blocks.prompt: The Rustiest Place We Know
blocks.text: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, and it is our closest neighbor that you could stand on. From Earth it looks like a small orange dot. Up close, it is a cold desert covered in red dust. The red comes from iron. The dust on Mars is full of iron that has rusted, the same way an old nail turns orange when it gets wet. The whole planet is coated in it. Mars is smaller than Earth. You would weigh about a third of what you weigh here, so a small hop would carry you high. A day on Mars is almost the same as ours, just forty minutes longer. But a year takes 687 Earth days, because Mars has a much longer trip around the Sun. Nobody has walked on Mars yet. Robots have. Rovers the size of cars drive across the rocks, drilling holes and taking pictures. They are looking for one thing above all: signs that water once flowed there, and maybe life with it.

blocks.prompt: A Planet That Dried Out
blocks.text: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and the only other world in our solar system where a robot has ever driven around. It is about half the width of Earth, and every inch of it is dry. The color has a simple explanation. Martian soil is loaded with iron, and that iron has rusted. Rust is iron plus oxygen, so the red of Mars is really the color of an old nail left out in the rain, spread across an entire planet. Wind lifts the fine rust dust into the sky, which is why the Martian sky glows a dull butterscotch instead of blue. Mars is a planet of extremes. Olympus Mons rises about 16 miles above the plains, close to three times the height of Mount Everest. A canyon called Valles Marineris runs 2,500 miles across the surface, deep enough to swallow the Grand Canyon several times over. Yet the air is so thin that standing there would feel closer to standing in empty space than on a mountaintop. It was not always like this. Cameras in orbit have photographed dried riverbeds branching across the dust. Rovers have rolled over rounded pebbles, the kind that only get smooth by tumbling in running water. Billions of years ago Mars had rivers, lakes, and a thicker sky. Then the planet's core cooled and its magnetic field faded. Without that shield, the solar wind stripped the air away a little at a time, and the water froze or escaped. Mars did not explode or die suddenly. It simply dried out, slowly, over a very long time. Finding out exactly how is why we keep sending robots.

notes: Entry speed on arrival: about 12,000 mph

blocks.prompt: Seven Minutes, No Help From Home
blocks.text: Getting a spacecraft to Mars is not the hard part. The hard part is stopping. A capsule arriving from Earth hits the top of the Martian atmosphere at roughly 12,000 miles per hour. It has about seven minutes to slow to zero and set a one-ton rover down gently on the rocks. Everything in those seven minutes has to work in the right order, at the right second, with no help from home. Radio signals take between about three and twenty-two minutes to cross the gap, depending on where the two planets are. By the time engineers on Earth hear that the capsule has touched the atmosphere, the landing is already over. It has either worked or it has not. They just do not know which yet. Mars makes this worse than it sounds. Its atmosphere is thick enough to set a heat shield glowing, but far too thin to do the braking a parachute could do on Earth. Less than one percent of Earth's air pressure means a parachute alone leaves the craft falling much too fast. So NASA stacks the tricks. A heat shield sheds most of the speed as fire. A supersonic parachute grabs what it can. Then the parachute is cut away and rockets take over, hovering the craft above the ground while it lowers the rover on cables like a package on a winch. The rocket stage then flies off to crash a safe distance away. It works, but not always. Roughly half of all missions ever sent to Mars have failed. Landers have burned up, bounced wrong, or gone silent on the way down. The ones that survive have been extraordinary. Opportunity was designed to last 90 days and lasted 14 years. Curiosity has been driving since 2012. In 2021, a helicopter named Ingenuity lifted off in air a hundred times thinner than ours and became the first machine to fly on another world. It was planned for five flights. It made 72. Every one of those machines is out there right now, still sitting where it stopped, waiting for people who have not arrived yet.

6.title: The Planet That Rusted Red
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Core dynamo shut down roughly 4 billion years ago

Jezero Crater holds an ancient river delta

Average temperature around 80 below zero Fahrenheit
Launch windows open only every 26 months

blocks.prompt: The Planet That Lost Its Air
blocks.text: Mars is the only planet we have ever found that used to be habitable and is not anymore. That single sentence is why it gets so much of our attention. Roughly four billion years ago, Mars looked far more like Earth than like the frozen desert it is now. It had a thicker atmosphere, clouds, rain or at least meltwater, rivers that cut branching valleys, and standing lakes that lasted long enough to lay down mud in flat layers. We are not guessing at this. Orbiters have mapped delta fans where rivers once emptied into basins. Curiosity has driven over conglomerate, a rock made of pebbles cemented together, with the pebbles rounded exactly the way stones are rounded by rolling along a streambed. Perseverance sits inside Jezero Crater specifically because the crater holds an ancient river delta, and river deltas are where fine sediment settles, and fine sediment is where evidence of life would be preserved if there ever was any. Then Mars lost. The most likely explanation begins deep inside it. Earth's molten iron core churns and generates a global magnetic field that reaches out past the atmosphere and deflects the solar wind, the constant stream of charged particles the Sun throws in every direction. Mars is smaller, so it cooled faster, and its core dynamo shut down. The magnetic shield went with it. After that, the solar wind spent billions of years peeling the Martian atmosphere away molecule by molecule. NASA's MAVEN orbiter has actually watched this happening, measuring gas escaping into space right now. As the air thinned, the pressure dropped, and liquid water stopped being possible on the surface. Water does not need heat alone to stay liquid. It needs something pressing down on it. Today the pressure on Mars is under one percent of Earth's, low enough that exposed water would boil and freeze almost at once. The water that remains is locked in the polar caps and buried as ice under the dust. This is the part worth sitting with. Mars did not lose its atmosphere in a catastrophe. There was no impact, no explosion, no single bad day. A planet with rivers became a planet without them through a process too slow for anyone to have noticed, driven by a change in its core that no surface observer could have seen. Habitability turned out to depend on plumbing nobody was looking at. People talk casually about moving to Mars if Earth goes wrong. It is worth being precise about what that would mean. The surface receives radiation with no magnetic field and almost no air to absorb it. The soil contains perchlorates, salts that are toxic to people. The average temperature is around eighty degrees below zero Fahrenheit. There is nothing to breathe. Every calorie, every drop of water, and every spare part would have to be grown, mined, or shipped across a gap that takes months to cross and opens only every twenty-six months. A ruined Earth would still be, by an enormous margin, the friendlier of the two. That is not an argument against going. Mars is the best laboratory we have for the question of whether life ever started anywhere but here, and answering that would change how we think about ourselves. But the honest reason to study Mars may be closer to home. It is the one nearby example of a world that was once warm and wet and is not anymore, and it did not need anyone's help to get that way.
